name: Hassan Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my uncle Karim's firm, Ibrahim Builders. It's small, four of us, and we do house extensions and loft conversions in the streets around town, the kind of job where a family wants a bigger kitchen or a bedroom in the roof. I do the carpentry mostly, floor joists, stud walls, the roof timbers for the loft, and I help with whatever else needs doing, plastering, a bit of tiling. We start at eight because Uncle Karim says you don't wake the neighbours before then. I like seeing a family move into a room we built. What wears me out is customers changing their mind halfway through, after the timber's cut.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged, Samira, we're getting married next summer, God willing. She works at a pharmacy counter. I live with my parents for now to save for the wedding and a deposit on a flat, but honestly I've got less than a month's worth saved, weddings cost more than you'd think. My uncle pays fair for a small firm but it's less than the big companies, and there aren't many building jobs round here if you're not family. I don't use AI, I don't trust it, and I don't need it to cut a joist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I expected, to be honest. They make big noise about computers and the work stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, that it was mostly talk from people who've never built anything. At the mosque on Friday, the older men would agree with me. I'm not really online, I'd maybe say it in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can get married and keep working for my uncle without worrying. That's what I want. A steady job, a wife, a family, the same as my father had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, same as now. Work for Uncle Karim, save every month for the wedding and the flat, and maybe start learning the business side from him, because one day he'll want to slow down. I wouldn't change anything for a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Peaceful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the business side. Is that something your uncle has talked about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a little. His sons went to university, they don't want to do building. He's said to me, Hassan, one day this is yours if you work for it. I take that seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the saving like, month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some months I put away two hundred, some months nothing, depends if a job finishes and he pays the bonus. Samira's family want a proper wedding, and I want to give them that. It's slow, but we'll get there.

S0.say: I'd say I knew it, that it was mostly talk from people who've never built anything. The older men at the mosque would agree, and I'd say it in the family group chat.
S0.think: Privately it means I can get married and keep working for my uncle without worrying. A steady job, a wife and a family, the same as my father had, is what I want.
S0.do: Keeps working for his uncle's firm and saves each month for the wedding and a flat deposit. Starts learning the business side so he can take over one day.
S0.quote: A steady job, a wife, a family, the same as my father had.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan's life plan is clear and traditional: marriage, family and one day taking over his uncle's firm. He openly distrusts AI and never uses it. This picture simply confirms that his plan holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Many jobs change, it says. I don't like the sound of that, but building is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good builders will always be needed and that people still want someone they can trust in their house. I'd say young people should learn a trade, not sit in front of a computer. I'd tell my cousins that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry a little about my uncle's business. If the big firms use computers to price jobs cheaper and faster, small firms like ours lose customers. My uncle does quotes by hand on a notepad, and people might go for the quicker one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and see what happened before I did anything. Maybe I'd suggest to my uncle that one of my younger cousins helps with the computer side for quotes, because I wouldn't do it. I'd save a bit harder for the wedding just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A small worry, like a crack in plaster you keep looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do the computer side. Why not, if it might help the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not what I'm good at, and I don't trust what it tells you. My cousin Yusuf is seventeen, he's on his phone all day, let him do it. I'll do the joists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if small firms like yours lost out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, mostly, and the tech people who sell them these things. But also customers who only look at price. My father always said you get what you pay for. When the cheap extension leaks, they'll call us.

S1.say: I'd say good builders will always be needed and people want someone they trust in their house. I'd tell my cousins to learn a trade instead of sitting at a computer.
S1.think: Privately I'd worry a little about my uncle's firm, because big companies using computers to price jobs faster and cheaper could take our customers. He still does quotes by hand on a notepad.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what happens before acting. Suggests a younger cousin handle computer quotes for the firm and saves harder for the wedding.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a crack in the plaster he keeps looking at.
S1.quote: When the cheap extension leaks, they'll call us.
S1.fieldNote: Hassan's public message is about trust and trades, while privately he worries about the family firm being undercut. He would hand any new technology to a teenage cousin rather than learn it. Blame falls on big companies, tech sellers and price-only customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And robots doing building work. I don't believe that, but if it's true, that's very bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who made this should have thought about families before they did it. I'd say it at the mosque and to my family. I wouldn't say the government should pay everyone, but I'd say these companies owe something to the people they replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be very scared. My uncle's firm couldn't buy robots, it's four men and two vans. If people can get a robot extension cheaper, we're finished, and I'd be finished with it, with a wedding booked and nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Samira and her family about making the wedding smaller, maybe at the community hall instead of the venue. I'd cut everything else. I'd lean on my family, we look after each other, and the mosque has people who help when someone loses work. I'd keep working for my uncle as long as there was any work at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray about it a lot, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a hard conversation with Samira's family. What would you actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I want to marry your daughter and I want to look after her, and right now looking after her means not spending money we don't have. Her father is a practical man, he ran a shop. I think he'd respect it, even if her mother cried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't want the government to pay everyone. Would you take help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, for a short time, yes. But I'd go to my family first, then the community. Taking handouts isn't how I was raised. I'd want work, any work.

S2.say: I'd say the people who made this should have thought about families first. I wouldn't say the government should pay everyone, but I'd say these companies owe something to the people they replaced.
S2.think: Privately I'd be very scared, because my uncle's four-man firm couldn't buy robots. If people could get a cheaper robot extension, we'd be finished, and I'd have a wedding booked and nothing saved.
S2.do: Asks Samira's family to make the wedding smaller, perhaps at the community hall, and cuts all other spending. Leans on family and the mosque community and keeps working for his uncle while any work remains.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and he would pray about it a lot.
S2.quote: I want to marry your daughter and I want to look after her, and right now looking after her means not spending money we don't have.
S2.fieldNote: Hassan meets this picture through his family and faith: smaller wedding, lean on family and community, keep working. He distinguishes clearly between family support and government handouts. His fear centres on the firm's future rather than his own skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast. But we'd be married by then, with a bit of luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to get ready, and that we can't wait for the government to fix it. I'd say young men should still learn a trade, because people will still want a person they trust for a while. I'd say it at the mosque, where people listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years worries me, because I'd want children by then. I'd have a wife, maybe a baby on the way, and no idea if my work would still be there. My uncle's firm might last a few years, but I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding plan but make it simpler, so we could save more for after. I'd save every month I could, aim for three months of money, and I'd keep working for Uncle Karim. If he decided to buy a machine, I'd help, but I'd be slow with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years sounds long but it isn't when you're starting a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd wait a year or two, to see. Samira wants children soon, and so do I. But I wouldn't want a baby and no job. We'd decide together, and we'd pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn, with five years, even if you don't like computers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the business side properly, quoting and dealing with customers, because a robot can't sit in someone's kitchen and listen. My uncle is good at that. People trust him. I'd learn that from him.

S3.say: I'd say families and communities need to get ready, because we can't wait for the government to fix it. I'd say young men should still learn a trade, since people will want someone they trust for a while.
S3.think: Privately five years worries me because I'd want children by then, with no idea whether my work would still be there. My uncle's firm might last a few years, but I don't know.
S3.do: Keeps the wedding but simplifies it to save more, and aims for three months of savings. Keeps working for his uncle, learns customer dealing and quoting from him, and may delay children by a year or two.
S3.feel: Anxious, because five years isn't long when starting a family.
S3.quote: A robot can't sit in someone's kitchen and listen.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Hassan's worry shifts from the wedding to starting a family, and he'd consider waiting a year or two for children. His idea of a safe skill is trust and customer care, learned from his uncle, not technology. He still places responsibility on families and community before government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. I'd be thirty-seven, with children, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people to prepare properly, and that families should stick together. I'd say we need more apprenticeships for young people in things robots can't do, whatever those are. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels more manageable. I'd have most of a decade of work with my uncle, maybe take over the firm. I'm still worried about the end, when a robot builds a whole extension, but people still want someone they know in their house, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, get married next summer as planned, and save steadily. I'd learn the business from my uncle so I could run the firm. I'd wait and see how fast the robots really come, because I've heard a lot of promises about machines that never came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. Far enough away that I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people want someone they know in their house. Would that hold, if robots are cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For some people, yes. Older people, families with children, people who don't like strangers or machines in their home. Maybe not enough to keep four men busy. Maybe enough for two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wedding with the whole family, and maybe a child before it comes. And a few years of savings. With two years, we'd be starting married life in a crisis.

S4.say: I'd say there's time to prepare properly and families should stick together. I'd say we need more apprenticeships for young people in work robots can't do, and I'd say it calmly.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels manageable, with most of a decade working for my uncle and maybe taking over the firm. I still worry about robots building whole extensions, but I think people still want someone they know in their house.
S4.do: Gets married next summer as planned, keeps working and saves steadily. Learns to run the firm from his uncle and waits to see how fast robots really arrive.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, far enough away to breathe.
S4.quote: With two years, we'd be starting married life in a crisis.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Hassan keep his life plan almost intact: wedding, children, and possibly the family firm. He bets on trust and personal relationships surviving, while admitting it might only keep two of the four men busy. His scepticism about promised machines also softens his worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be starting married life with nothing. What would help is apprenticeships and real work, not handouts, and some help for small family firms so they're not crushed by the big companies. And my family, of course. They're the first help I'd ask for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens, I believe there's a plan bigger than mine. That doesn't stop me worrying, but it stops me falling apart. My father lost his job once when I was ten, and that's how he got through it.

headlineQuote: That doesn't stop me worrying, but it stops me falling apart.
portrait: Hassan Ibrahim is a 27-year-old carpenter in his uncle's four-man firm building house extensions and loft conversions, engaged to Samira, living with his parents and holding less than a month of savings ahead of next summer's wedding. He distrusts AI, never uses it, and would hand any new technology to a younger cousin. He is calm about the plateau, uneasy about big firms undercutting the family business, and alarmed at AGI in two years, when he'd shrink the wedding and lean on family and the mosque community. With more time his worry moves to starting a family, and he bets on trust and customer care as the skills a robot can't replace.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he would be starting married life with nothing.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and real work rather than handouts, support for small family firms against big companies, and his own family's help first.
